title: Judging frameworks: why ugly, asymmetric models beat pretty ones
summary: Jason Cohen argues that business models and frameworks, like physics theories, can be useful without being correct, but the useful ones try to capture the messy real world. Symmetric, tidy diagrams and round-number lists are red flags that a framework was built for slides and consulting pitches rather than reality.

principles.text: A model can be useful (predictive) without being correct, so judge models by whether they help you decide, not by how true they sound.
principles.quote: Their model was _wrong_ in describing the universe, but _useful_ in predicting eclipses.

principles.text: Test a framework by asking if it models the messy real world or just looks nice in presentations and consultants' materials.
principles.quote: Does the framework attempt to model the messy real world, or does it seem like a pretty fantasy that looks nice in presentations, HBR articles, and consultants' sales materials?

principles.text: Distrust frameworks about people packaged in symmetric diagrams with identical counts of bullets and subcategories.
principles.quote: I immediately disbelieve any framework about human beings that comes packaged in a nice, symmetric diagram, with identical quantities of bullets and sub-categories

principles.text: A list with exactly ten items is a red flag; a list should contain however many items actually make sense.
principles.quote: Another red flag is any list with exactly 10 items. That's how many fingers we have, not how many things should probably be on that list.

principles.text: Models of organizations must reflect real human incentives, emotions and personalities, not treat people as fungible, predictable worker-units.
principles.quote: is it modeled as if people are fungible worker-units with predictable responses to stimuli, built by a professor who has never managed a team beyond six sycophantic grad students?

principles.text: Good strategy models grapple with interacting, dynamic systems rather than one rubric of 2x2s applied identically to every company.
principles.quote: I trust more in diagrams that are imbalanced, asymmetrical, or even ugly, because perhaps they're primarily interested in modeling the messy truth of the world
